slides: Open by framing coordinates as a choice of language rather than a mere grid. The chapter moves among Cartesian, polar, conic, tangent, circular, hyperbolic, spiral, and three-dimensional coordinates, and the main question is which language makes each geometric invariant easiest to see.

Use the route slide to keep the many coordinate topics connected. The lecture starts with a dictionary for conics and tangents, then treats arc length and area as limiting coordinate measurements, compares circular and hyperbolic parameters, studies an equiangular spiral, and ends with quadrics and classification.

The coordinate dictionary slide is about translation across representations. A conic can be read from Cartesian coefficients, polar placement, tangent data, or a discriminant sign. The tangent dot gradient residual shows that the line drawn as tangent is actually perpendicular to the gradient.

The arc length and area slide should stress approximation with memory. Polygonal secants approximate perimeter, and shoelace determinants approximate area. As the sample count increases, the area error shrinks and the polygon length approaches the independent Ramanujan estimate for the ellipse.

Circular and hyperbolic functions appear here as coordinate systems for sector geometry. The identities look parallel, but one lives on the circle and the other on the rectangular hyperbola. The derivative checks explain why the visual analogy has algebraic force.

The equiangular spiral slide makes a coordinate curve into a self-similar object. The tangent keeps a constant angle with the radius vector, and rotating the curve corresponds to scaling it by predictable factors, so polar coordinates reveal structure hidden in Cartesian plotting.

Three-dimensional coordinates expand the chapter from planar curves to surfaces. A tangent plane to the sphere is checked by a zero residual, while the ruled quadric lab shows two families of straight lines sweeping a curved surface. Coordinates become a construction tool.

The quadratic lab turns coordinate choice into a classifier. The discriminant separates elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic cases, but the suggested coordinate view also tells students how to inspect the geometry: scaled axes, tangent direction, asymptote frame, or rotated principal axes.

This synthesis slide is for avoiding a common misconception: coordinates are not the geometry itself. A good coordinate system preserves the object while making one feature simple, such as a tangent, an area determinant, a constant angle, a ruling family, or a conic type.

Close by returning to the chapter's practical lesson. Coordinates are chosen instruments: discriminants classify conics, determinant sums approximate area, circular and hyperbolic parameters encode sectors, polar coordinates reveal spiral self-similarity, and 3D coordinates expose tangent planes and ruled surfaces.
